**(2) Approaches message**

Before the approaches, one missing dependency carries forward. The 10k-rows-in-under-60s row needs paged row retrieval. The gather draft looked it up and found paging unimplemented, so it has to be built. Whether 60s is achievable is still unverified, because no timing exists. The spec will name a timing test as the proof and list the target under Open Questions until that test runs.

The approaches differ on where rows come from and where the CSV is assembled. You answered that export uses the visible table columns in table order, with the button beside the report title.

**Recommended - reuse the serializer, add paged retrieval.** The Export CSV button fetches the report in pages and feeds each page into the existing serializer in src/export/csv.ts. The serializer is driven by the table's column definitions, so the export matches the visible columns and their order by construction. The 10k-row volume is handled page by page instead of in one load. The cost is new paging code plus a serializer that accepts rows incrementally. The serializer's other callers see only a widened input type.
Removes: none
Adds: Export CSV button beside the report title on the reports page; paged row-fetch helper; incremental/iterable row input on the src/export/csv.ts serializer; tests for column parity, button presence, and 10k-row timing
Pattern: follows src/export/csv.ts's use of the table's column definitions as the single column source, and extends that shared path instead of copying it beside the caller.

**Reuse-only - serialize the rows the table already holds.** The button hands the table's current rows and column definitions to src/export/csv.ts as they are, with no new construct. This is the smallest change. Its gap is the 10k-row row: without paging, either the table holds all 10k rows in memory or the export covers only what is loaded. Neither path has evidence that it meets the 60s row.
Removes: none
Adds: Export CSV button beside the report title
Pattern: follows src/export/csv.ts. It leaves the ticket's volume row resting on an unmeasured full load.

**Drop the client-side assumption - server-side export.** The ask implies that export is assembled from the page's table. A server endpoint could instead stream the CSV, so the browser only downloads. This scales best and fits a later mailer hand-off. However, it duplicates column ordering on the server, apart from the table definitions that serve as the column source.
Removes: none
Adds: export endpoint; server-side column mapping; download button beside the report title; endpoint and timing tests
Pattern: cuts across src/export/csv.ts's table-definition column source by adding a second column path.

I recommend the first approach. It is the only one that keeps a single column source and also gives the 60s row a concrete mechanism. The recommendation would flip to reuse-only if a lookup showed the table already loads full reports and 10k rows serialize in under 60s. It would flip to server-side if the paged client export failed the timing test.

B) In the table toolbar.
C) Other - name it.
Recommendation: A - it makes export discoverable as a report-level action.

---

### Approaches message — after the recorded answers

The agreed presentation is a button beside the report title, exporting visible table columns in table order. The recorded implementation choice is to reuse the existing CSV serializer and add paging.

The supplied draft reports that paging is unimplemented. The report-loading API’s ability to retrieve successive pages remains unverified because no primary-code lookup is available. The serializer’s handling of visible-column order and the representative 10k-row benchmark setup are likewise unverified. These are implementation and verification dependencies; they do not justify cutting the performance criterion.

**I recommend approach A, consistent with your recorded choice.** The distinguishing axis is where complete-report retrieval and export execution live.

**A) Extend the existing report/export paths with paging and serializer reuse.** Keep the button on the reports page, retrieve all report pages through the existing report-loading boundary, and pass the agreed visible-column sequence to the existing serializer. This is the minimal reuse-only candidate: paging adds behavior to existing paths rather than introducing a separate export subsystem.

Its main risks are whether the data API supports complete retrieval, how paging behaves if report data changes during export, and whether retrieval plus serialization meets the stated performance target. Existing serializer callers must retain their behavior.

Removes: none.
Adds: report-title button and handler; paging behavior in the existing report-loading path; visible-column/order wiring into the existing serializer; completeness, column-order, failure, and 10k-row timing tests. Exact owning files beyond the serializer require verification.
Pattern: extends the shared CSV path identified at `src/export/csv.ts` rather than duplicating serialization beside the reports page.

**B) Move export execution behind a server-side export endpoint, still reusing the serializer.** This drops the unconfirmed assumption that the browser must retrieve and serialize the complete report. The button requests an export, while the server retrieves pages and produces the downloadable CSV.

This offers a clearer boundary for larger exports, but adds a public endpoint and server-side responsibilities. Its viability depends on whether `src/export/csv.ts` can run in that environment; the supplied evidence does not establish that. It is not the recorded choice and would require your approval before adoption.

Removes: none.
Adds: export endpoint and contract; server-side paged retrieval and response handling; report-title button and client request handling; endpoint, authorization, completeness, column-order, failure, and timing tests.
Pattern: preserves reuse of `src/export/csv.ts`, but introduces a new execution boundary whose necessity is not yet demonstrated.

I would switch from A to B only if verified API, runtime, or performance evidence shows that the existing client-side path cannot meet the approved requirements.
